items.title: New York bans AI chatbot toys – but not in time for Christmas
items.description: Talking teddies that describe massacres and help kids break bedtime rules? New York has had enough, and has banned AI chatbot toys for five years. Just not in time for Christmas. Read more in my article on the Hot for Security blog.

items.title: Smashing Security podcast #494: The Russian accused of spying on Palantir from Starbucks
items.description: A would-be spy is recruited on Telegram for $15,000 and sent halfway around the world to snoop on Palantir. His cover story when he's caught? He wanted to ask a woman out on a date. Meanwhile, Carl Miller investigates a think tank with 300 experts on its books, one of whom is the inconveniently dead Henry Kissinger. But who is its real audience? You might be surprised. Plus, Coreview's Andrea Sivieri explains why Microsoft Copilot is brilliant at finding anything in your company, including the salary spreadsheet someone shared with everybody back in 2019. All this and more in episode 494 of the "Smashing Security" podcast with cybersecurity expert and keynote speaker Graham Cluley, and special guest Carl Miller.

items.title: Signal blocks AI assistants from snooping on your encrypted messages
items.description: Signal is blocking Siri and Gemini from reading your encrypted chats off the screen, and warning that AI agents built into operating systems are an "existential threat" to privacy. Read more in my article on the Hot for Security blog.

items.title: n0n extortion gang leaks data of JPMorgan Chase, Visa, and Mastercard customers
items.description: Data belonging to customers of three of the biggest companies in global finance has been leaked online, after hackers breached third-party service providers working for JPMorgan Chase, Visa, and Mastercard. Read more in my article on the Hot for Security blog.

items.title: Cold Relic: What you need to know
items.description: A Russian spy group is breaking into organisations by pretending to be people they already trust. Meet Cold Relic, the hackers formerly known as COLDRIVER. Read more in my article on the Fortra blog.

items.title: Smashing Security podcast #493: Why your AI model could be a sleeper agent
items.description: You join a video call, and your contact and a few colleagues are already there, waiting patiently. But they can't hear you, and a pop-up says you need to install an update to fix your microphone. What could possibly go wrong? Meanwhile, we explain how changing just a handful of numbers can turn an AI model into a sleeper agent, waiting for the right moment to strike. Plus, Andrius Buinovskis of NordLayer explains how companies can see which AI tools their staff are really using, and stop sensitive data leaking out, without banning AI altogether. All this and more in episode 493 of the "Smashing Security" podcast with cybersecurity expert and keynote speaker Graham Cluley, and special guest Ray Redacted.

items.title: WhiteArmor gang claims responsibility for latest cyber attack on shipping giant Maersk
items.description: Shipping giant Maersk has confirmed that one of its systems was broken into by hackers who have stolen data. The WhiteArmor gang has claimed responsbility for the attack. Read more in my article on the Hot for Security blog.

items.title: Smashing Security podcast #492: How hackers turned Russian cars into pumpkins
items.description: You're driving your new Chinese SUV when the dashboard goes dark. Ten minutes later, your phone rings. A stranger says they've got the digital key to your car, and would you like it back? Of course you would. That'll be $550. Meanwhile, three men have been charged over a scheme that used deepfakes of company bosses to steal around $130 million. Hear more about what happened, and the simple human trick that can foil the fakes. All this and more in episode 492 of the "Smashing Security" podcast with cybersecurity expert and keynote speaker Graham Cluley, and special guest Danny Palmer.

items.title: Iranian hackers turned up the heat on French supermarket freezers, says France
items.description: Iran has been officially accused by France of being responsible for cyber attacks last month that meddled with supermarket freezers, causing some to catch fire. Read more in my article on the Hot for Security blog.

items.title: Smashing Security podcast #491: How AI agents are spooking the banks
items.description: Bank of America has a message for its customers: please, for the love of God, stop handing your banking passwords to your AI assistant. And if your robot does something daft with your money? That's your problem, not theirs. Meanwhile, a company that promised to rescue ransomware victims without paying the criminals stands accused of... paying the criminals. ProPublica's Renee Dudley was on the case years before the indictment. Plus, Dropzone AI's Edward Wu asks what happens when AI models break out of their test environment and go hacking, and whether AI agents can help overstretched security teams keep up. All this and more in episode 491 of the "Smashing Security" podcast with cybersecurity expert and keynote speaker Graham Cluley, and special guest Renee Dudley.

items.title: Hackers leak personnel data of 41,000+ Homeland Security staff, including ICE and border agents
items.description: The US Department of Homeland Security has had the details of more than 41,000 staff, including ICE and CBP agents, published online. Not ideal for an organisation with "Security" in its name. Read more in my article on the Hot for Security blog.

items.title: BYOD cyberattack diverts ambulances and cancels classes at University of New Mexico health center
items.description: Ambulances were diverted, surgeries cancelled, and medical students sent home from classes after a ransomware group attacked the University of New Mexico's Health Sciences Center (HSC) this week. Read more in my article on the Fortra blog.

items.title: Smashing Security podcast #490: How Jared Kushner’s iPhone was allegedly hacked twice
items.description: Dutch spies, Russian hackers and Jared Kushner’s iPhone. It sounds like the ingredients for a thriller, but according to claims in a new book the US President's son-in-law may have been hacked twice. Is any of it true, and what does it tell us about the phones in our pockets? Meanwhile, James Ball explains that of the internet’s most trusted security keys were protected by numbers so small that one of them was... four. Yes, "4". And then, of course, to make the week worse we suffered a PHPocalpyse... Plus, Chuck Randolph of 360 Privacy explains how the internet has made it scarily easy to put company executives and public officials in danger. All this and more in episode 490 of the “Smashing Security” podcast with cybersecurity expert and keynote speaker Graham Cluley, and special guest James Ball.

items.title: Hive ransomware affiliate jailed, years after FBI infiltrated the gang’s systems
items.description: A Ukrainian man who carried out ransomware attacks for both the Nefilim and Hive gangs, including attacks on law firms and a healthcare provider during the COVID-19 pandemic, has been sentenced to 70 months in a US prison. Read more in my article on the Hot for Security blog.

items.title: Hacker leaks 281 GB of data from Germany’s far-right AfD party
items.description: The AfD has confirmed that hackers breached its hosting provider. A leak site now claims to offer 421,179 of the party’s internal emails, and shows AI-written summaries rather than the emails themselves. Read more in my article on the Hot for Security blog.

items.title: Smashing Security podcast #489: How a brand new crypto wallet came with a spy inside
items.description: Imagine buying a brand new hardware wallet for your cryptocurrency with the shrink-wrap still on... what could possibly be hiding inside? We break out a Geiger counter and a cat to find out. Meanwhile, malicious ads are targeting journalists with zero-click attacks. Plus, Origin’s Spencer Thompson reveals what AI agents are really getting up to on your employees’ laptops when nobody’s looking. All this and more in episode 489 of the “Smashing Security” podcast with cybersecurity expert and keynote speaker Graham Cluley, and special guest Lianne Potter.

items.title: Police arrest Qilin ransomware suspect on holiday, as links made to Synnovis hack that contributed to patient’s death
items.description: A 28-year-old Russian man has been arrested by German police, suspected of being a key member of the Qilin ransomware gang. Detectives have linked the man to the attack against blood-testing firm Synnovis, that disrupted London hospitals, and resulted in the death of a patient. Read more in my article on the Hot for Security blog.

items.title: Irish police force has its Twitter hacked in cryptocurrency scam
items.description: There must have been red faces in the social media department of Ireland's police headquarters after two of its accounts were hijacked this week. Read more in my article on the Hot for Security blog.

items.title: Krybit ransomware: what you need to know
items.description: Krybit is a fast-growing ransomware gang that was hacked by a rival, hit back, and is still extorting victims. Find out how it works, who it has targeted, and what organisations can do to protect themselves. Read more in my article on the Fortra blog.

items.title: Smashing Security podcast #488: How a ransomware negotiator ended up arrested at his own conference
items.description: A ransomware negotiator attended a cybersecurity conference, only to be arrested by the FBI in connection with its investigation into the ShinyHunters gang. Meanwhile, hackers get the keys to ASOS's app and the chance to message every single customer. What did they say? And how did the company respond? We have thoughts. All this and more is discussed in episode 488 of the "Smashing Security" podcast with cybersecurity expert and keynote speaker Graham Cluley, and special guest Paul Ducklin.
